guide.title: Unit 8: Style, comparisons, and audience: review guide
guide.intro: Style is the sum of a writer's choices: words, comparisons, and sentence structures. This unit practices explaining how those choices shape how an audience perceives the writer and the argument, and making them yourself.

sections.title: Choices for an audience
body: Comparisons (analogies, metaphors, examples) work only if the audience knows the thing being compared to. A comparison to a sports team may persuade fans and lose readers who don't follow sports.
Every choice, from formality to examples, signals who the writer thinks the audience is. A mismatch can make a writer seem condescending or out of touch.
points: Choose comparisons from the audience's experience.
Formal settings call for precise, measured language.

sections.title: Word choice and perception
body: Diction (word choice) shapes the writer's persona: technical terms can show expertise but may alienate non-experts; casual words can seem friendly or unserious depending on the setting.
Connotation matters: “stubborn” and “determined” describe similar behavior with opposite judgments.
points: Ask how each word makes the writer seem: careful, angry, trustworthy?
Define technical terms for general audiences.

sections.title: Style and sentence structure
body: Sentence length and structure create emphasis: a short sentence after several long ones lands hard; repetition and parallelism make ideas memorable; questions invite the audience to think along.
Style should serve the argument: a dramatic style can move an audience at a rally but may seem overblown in a report.
points: Anaphora (repeating an opening phrase) builds emphasis.
Short sentences emphasize; long ones elaborate.

example.prompt: Choose a comparison to explain compound interest to a group of tenth graders.
example.solution: “Compound interest is like a snowball rolling downhill: the bigger it gets, the more snow it picks up each turn.” It uses an image the audience knows and captures how growth builds on growth.

misconceptions: “Fancy words always make a writer sound smart.”
Words that don't fit the audience can make a writer seem pretentious or unclear.
Style shapes how an audience receives the argument.
Comparisons depend on what the audience knows.

passages.title: Passage 1: From a graduation speech to a community college class
text: (1) Many of you took the long way here. You worked the early shift, then came to class. You fed your children, then opened your textbooks. You missed the bus, then caught the next one.
(2) Some people think the long way is the wrong way. They are mistaken. The long way is where you learned to budget an hour like a paycheck, to treat a deadline like a shift you could not miss.

(3) Today you have finished. Tomorrow, someone at your job, at your kitchen table, or at the next bus stop will ask how you did it. Tell them. That is how the long way becomes a road for someone else.

passages.title: Passage 2: A scientist's letter to state legislators
text: (1) Dear Members of the Committee: I write as a hydrologist who has measured groundwater in Harlan County for fifteen years. The data show a steady decline: wells that reached water at forty feet in 2010 now reach it at sixty-five.
(2) To put this in terms of a household budget: the county has been spending its savings faster than it deposits them. Every dry year draws down the account further.

(3) I respectfully ask the committee to fund a two-year study of recharge rates before approving new large-scale pumping permits. The data I have described do not settle every question, but they are reason enough for caution.

passages.title: Draft 1: A student paragraph for a middle-school assembly
text: The following is a draft of remarks a high school student will give to sixth graders about joining after-school clubs. It may need revision.

(1) Joining a club can seem scary. (2) Joining a club is like choosing a diversified portfolio of extracurricular assets. (3) You meet people who like what you like. (4) You also learn skills you won't learn in class. (5) My first club was the robotics team.

passages.title: Draft 2: A student email to a city parks director
text: The following is a draft of an email a student plans to send to the city's parks director. It may need revision.

(1) Hey! (2) The basketball courts at Lincoln Park are a total disaster and nobody in charge cares. (3) The backboards are cracked, and two rims have been missing since March. (4) Our team practices there three days a week. (5) Please fix the courts.

questions.prompt: Paragraph 1 repeats the pattern “You … , then …” several times. What is the main effect?
choices: It builds a rhythm that stresses the many obstacles the graduates overcame
It introduces statistics about how many of the graduates worked while studying
It confuses the audience about the order in which events happened
It shows that the speaker disapproves of the graduates' slow progress
questions.explanation: The parallel sentences pile up examples of the graduates' persistence.
choiceExplanations: There are no statistics.
The pattern makes the sequence clearer.
The tone is admiring.

questions.prompt: The comparisons in paragraph 2 (budgeting an hour “like a paycheck,” a deadline “like a shift”) are chosen mainly because
choices: they draw on the working lives many in the audience share
they show that the audience should quit their jobs to study full time
they describe the speaker's own childhood and first jobs
they come from scientific research on how adults manage time
questions.explanation: The speaker has just said many graduates work; comparisons from work connect to their experience.
choiceExplanations: They praise the skills work taught.
They describe the audience, not the speaker.
They are everyday comparisons, not research.

questions.prompt: What is the effect of the short sentences “They are mistaken.” and “Tell them.”?
choices: They summarize statistics about how the graduates succeeded
They deliver the speaker's key judgments with emphasis
They show that the speaker is unsure of what to say next
They change the subject from the graduates to the speaker
questions.explanation: After longer sentences, the short ones land as firm, memorable statements.
choiceExplanations: There are no statistics.
They sound certain.
They advance the same subject.

questions.prompt: How does the final sentence connect the speech's choices to its purpose?
choices: It shifts the speech's audience from the graduates to their employers and the coworkers they see at their jobs
It contradicts paragraph 2's claim that the long way taught the graduates valuable skills
It turns “the long way,” first presented as a hardship, into something that can help others, giving graduates a role
It suggests that the long way should be avoided by the people who ask the graduates for advice
questions.explanation: The repeated phrase gains a new meaning, ending with a call to action that suits a graduation audience.
choiceExplanations: The graduates remain the audience.
It builds on paragraph 2's praise.
It celebrates the long way.

questions.prompt: In paragraph 1, why does the writer mention being a hydrologist who has measured groundwater for fifteen years?
choices: To tell a personal story about the writer's career that is unrelated to the argument
To establish expertise and credibility with the committee
To ask the committee for a job running the study
To criticize the committee for ignoring groundwater data
questions.explanation: Stating qualifications up front makes the data more trustworthy to legislators.
choiceExplanations: The credentials support the argument.
The letter asks for a study, not a job.
The tone is respectful, not critical.

questions.prompt: Why does the writer compare the groundwater to a household budget in paragraph 2?
choices: To argue that households in Harlan County use too much water each year
To make a technical trend easy for non-scientist legislators to grasp
To show off technical vocabulary about aquifers and recharge rates
To change the topic to the county's taxes and spending
questions.explanation: A familiar comparison translates the data into terms the audience already understands.
choiceExplanations: The comparison is about the county's groundwater as a whole.
The comparison avoids technical vocabulary.
Taxes and spending aren't discussed; the budget is a comparison.

questions.prompt: Which best describes the writer's tone in paragraph 3?
choices: Despairing and hopeless
Playful and joking
Angry and accusing
Respectful and measured
questions.explanation: “I respectfully ask” and “do not settle every question” sound careful and courteous.
choiceExplanations: The writer proposes a constructive step.
The subject is treated seriously.
The writer doesn't accuse anyone.

questions.prompt: In paragraph 3, the writer admits the data “do not settle every question.” How does this choice likely affect the committee's view of the writer?
choices: It makes the writer seem uninformed about the groundwater data
It shows that the writer opposes the study and favors approving new pumping permits
It makes the writer seem honest and careful, which strengthens the request
It contradicts the data on falling water levels presented in paragraph 1
questions.explanation: Acknowledging the data's limits matches a scientist's careful persona and fits a request for more study.
choiceExplanations: Admitting limits signals expertise, not ignorance.
The writer is requesting the study.
It qualifies, not contradicts, the data.

questions.prompt: Sentence (2) uses a comparison that is poorly suited to sixth graders. Why?
choices: It is too short to explain what joining a club involves
It uses a question the sixth graders cannot answer yet
It relies on financial terms most sixth graders don't know
It mentions robotics, which just some of the sixth graders like
questions.explanation: “Diversified portfolio of extracurricular assets” assumes knowledge of investing.
choiceExplanations: Length isn't the problem; the vocabulary is.
It isn't a question.
It doesn't mention robotics.

questions.prompt: Which replacement for sentence (2) best suits the audience?
choices: Joining a club is like finding a lunch table where everyone likes the same things you do.
Joining a club is a decision with numerous ramifications for your social and academic future.
Joining a club is a strategic investment in human capital that pays dividends for years.
Clubs exist.
questions.explanation: A lunch-table comparison comes from sixth graders' everyday experience.
choiceExplanations: This is vague and formal.
This is even more abstract and financial.
This offers no comparison.

questions.prompt: The writer wants to combine sentences (3) and (4) to show that both benefits matter. Which is best?
choices: You meet people who like what you like, which is something you won't learn in any of your classes.
You meet people who like what you like, and you learn skills you won't learn in class.
You meet people who like what you like you learn skills you won't learn in class.
Meeting people who like what you like, and skills you won't learn in class.
questions.explanation: “And” joins two equally important benefits in a clear, grammatical sentence.
choiceExplanations: This illogically says that meeting people is something learned in class.
This is a run-on sentence.
This is a fragment with no main verb.

questions.prompt: Sentence (5) ends the paragraph abruptly. Which revision would best make the speaker seem relatable to sixth graders while supporting the point?
choices: Robots are machines that many students enjoy building in clubs after school.
My first club was the robotics team, which won several regional competitions while I served as its captain and leader.
My first club was the robotics team.
My first club was the robotics team; on the first day I knew no one, and by spring those were the people I ate lunch with.
questions.explanation: Sharing the same nervousness the audience feels makes the speaker relatable and illustrates the benefit.
choiceExplanations: This is irrelevant.
Boasting about being captain distances the speaker from nervous sixth graders.
This is unchanged.

questions.prompt: How is the writer likely to be perceived because of sentences (1) and (2)?
choices: As too informal and accusatory for an email to a city official
As respectful and formal, which suits a city official
As neutral and objective about the courts
As an expert in building and maintaining public sports facilities
questions.explanation: “Hey!” and “nobody in charge cares” may make the director defensive.
choiceExplanations: The language is casual and accusing.
The tone is charged, not neutral.
Nothing shows expertise.

questions.prompt: Which revision of sentence (2) best suits the audience while keeping the writer's concern?
choices: Nobody at the parks department cares about the Lincoln Park courts except our team.
The courts at Lincoln Park are, like, kind of bad and stuff.
I am writing about the basketball courts at Lincoln Park, which need repairs.
The courts at Lincoln Park are trash, and everyone knows it.
questions.explanation: A clear, polite statement of purpose suits an email to a city official.
choiceExplanations: This still accuses.
This is too casual and vague.
This is insulting.

questions.prompt: Which detail in the email would most likely persuade the parks director to act?
choices: Sentence (2), because it shows strong feelings
Sentence (1), because it greets the director
Sentence (5), because it is short and gets straight to the point
Sentence (3), because it describes specific, verifiable damage
questions.explanation: Specific damage gives the director a clear problem to send crews to fix.
choiceExplanations: Strong feelings without evidence may backfire.
A greeting isn't persuasive evidence.
Brevity alone doesn't persuade.
questions.licenseOrRights: Original question written for StudySprint. The unit's title and topics come from the linked College Board course page and the course's Course and Exam Description, as recorded in StudySprint's course outline (checked 2026-11-08); they were used only to confirm scope.

questions.prompt: Which revision of sentence (5) gives the request the most effective emphasis for this audience?
choices: PLEASE FIX THE COURTS AT LINCOLN PARK NOW, BEFORE ANOTHER SEASON IS RUINED FOR EVERYONE!!!
Fix the courts this month, or our team will tell everyone in town that the parks director simply doesn't care.
Courts.
Repairing the backboards and replacing the two rims before summer would let our team and other families play safely.
questions.explanation: A specific, polite request that names the benefit to the community gives the director a reason to act.
choiceExplanations: Capital letters and exclamation points seem rude.
A threat would alienate the director.
A one-word fragment doesn't make a request.
